title: Detachment from things
hook: not owning nothing, but not being owned by things

segments.voice: Yesterday, muhasabah, the evening ledger, and your line: count before counted. When you opened the accounts last night, which column was easier to fill? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

A reed mat on a floor. That's the whole scene in a hadith from the collection of al-Tirmidhi. The Prophet ﷺ gets up from sleeping on it, and the weave has left marks pressed into his side. His companions offer to make him a proper bed. His answer is a picture. What have I to do with this world? He is in it, he says, like a rider who stops in the shade of a tree, rests a while, then rides on and leaves the tree behind. Nothing about the tree is bad. The shade is real. But the rider doesn't move in. Today, the station that rider stands for.
screen: `A REED MAT, MARKS ON HIS SIDE.` → `A RIDER IN THE SHADE.` → `HE DOESN'T MOVE IN.`

segments.voice: The word is zuhd. It's usually put into English as renunciation, or detachment, and both can mislead. Renunciation sounds like an empty room and a cave. But another hadith in al-Tirmidhi defines zuhd in the world, and it starts with two things zuhd is not. It is not making the lawful forbidden, and it is not throwing your wealth away. Instead, it's being more sure of what is in Allah's hand than of what is in your own hand. So zuhd is not measured by what's in your house. It's measured by where your heart is resting. A person with very little can be gripped by the little they have. A person with a lot can hold it loosely. The Qur'an names the test, in Pickthall's translation: "That ye grieve not for the sake of that which hath escaped you, nor yet exult because of that which hath been given." Read it as a gauge. If losing a thing would flatten you, and gaining it makes you giddy, the thing has a grip on you. If you can be glad of it and let it go, you own it, and it doesn't own you. A line people repeat in the tradition, without one sure source, says zuhd is not owning nothing, but being owned by nothing. And there's a promise attached. In the collection of Ibn Majah, a man asks for a deed that will make Allah and people love him. The answer: be detached from the world, and Allah will love you. Be detached from what people have, and people will love you. Nobody likes a friend who's always eyeing their things.
screen: `NOT AN EMPTY ROOM.` · `MORE SURE OF ALLAH'S HAND THAN YOURS.` · `DON'T GRIEVE, DON'T GLOAT.` · then, large: `OWNED BY NOTHING.`

segments.voice: The practice: let one thing go. Settle, and breathe. Walk through your home in your mind, slowly. A closet. A drawer. A shelf in the garage. Look for one thing you haven't used in a long time but keep anyway. A jacket, a book, a pan, a cable. When you find it, notice the small tug that says, but what if I need it. Don't argue with the tug. Just notice it. Then ask who could use this thing now. A neighbor, a shelter, a friend. If you pray, you can recall the rider in the shade. If not, just let the picture of the thing leaving your hands sit for a moment. The bell holds the time.
Zuhd. Detachment: trusting what is in Allah's hand more than what is in your own, so that things can be enjoyed without taking hold of you. Today's word.
Your line: not owned by it. Today, actually give away the thing you found, and notice how long the tug lasts once it's gone. Tomorrow, patience, again. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-three.

howItsDone: Muslim teachers describe zuhd as an inner detachment rather than poverty: people keep their homes, work and wealth while trying to hold them loosely, and some practice it by regularly giving away what they no longer use.

fork.setup: the Prophet ﷺ wakes with the marks of a reed mat on his side, and his companions offer to make him a proper bed. what does he say?
options: yes, a soft bed would be good.
what have I to do with this world? I'm like a rider resting in shade.
fork.reveal: he answers with a picture: a rider who rests in a tree's shade, then rides on and leaves it. not a rule against comfort, a way of holding it.

original.note: Arabic: detachment, doing without, wanting little of the world.

trapdoor: what you thought: zuhd is giving everything away and living in a cave.
what it means: holding the world loosely, glad of what comes, not crushed by what goes.
what a scholar hears: the definition in al-Tirmidhi, not forbidding the lawful or wasting wealth, but being more sure of what is in Allah's hand than what is in your own.
recall: a pool or basin for drinking
